South
SOUTH
n. and adj. (rendering Hebrew negeb, tēmān, and dārōm, Greek notos)
From Old English sūth, the sun-side, cognate with sun — for an observer in the northern latitudes the sun stands in the southern sky. Hebrew has three words, each with its own flavour: negeb means the parched or dry country, and is the proper name of the arid region south of Judah, which is why the KJV can say a man went up out of Egypt into the south; tēmān means the right hand, the observer facing east; and dārōm is the bright quarter.

Biblical Definition

South in Scripture is the dry country, the right hand of a man facing the sunrise, and one of the four quarters from which God gathers His people. The patriarchal narratives use it as a place before it is a direction: Abram, driven to Egypt by famine, returns by the same road — “And Abram went up out of Egypt, he, and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the south” (Gen 13:1) — the Negeb being the parched approach to Canaan from Egypt. The word then takes on a theological weight in the psalm that denies every human ladder of advancement: “For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south” (Psa 75:6). The sentence stops short deliberately. Three quarters are named and the fourth is not, because the psalmist will not say that promotion comes from the north either — the next verse supplies the answer that is not a direction at all: but God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another. No point of the compass, no patron, no journey, no alliance lifts a man; God does. And the south stands in the roll of the quarters from which the elect are gathered to the feast: “And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God” (Luk 13:29). It is also the direction of obedience in an unlikely errand, when Philip is sent from a revival to a desert road: “Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert” (Act 8:26).

Webster 1828 Definition

The point of the compass opposite the north; in Hebrew the dry country, the Negeb south of Judah, and the right hand of one facing east; and in Scripture one of the four quarters from which the redeemed are gathered.

expand to see more

SOUTH, n. 1. One of the cardinal points, being the point of the horizon directly opposite to the north.

2. A southern region, country, or place; as, the queen of the south. Matt. 12.

3. adj. Being in a point toward the south; as the south side, the south border, the south wind.

4. In Hebrew, the parched or dry region; the Negeb, lying south of Judah, whence to go into the south is to go into that country.

5. In Scripture, promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south. Psalm 75. They shall come from the north, and from the south. Luke 13.

Key Scripture

Genesis 13:1 — "And Abram went up out of Egypt, he, and his wife, and all that he had, and Lot with him, into the south."

Psalm 75:6 — "For promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south."

Luke 13:29 — "And they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south, and shall sit down in the kingdom of God."

Acts 8:26 — "And the angel of the Lord spake unto Philip, saying, Arise, and go toward the south unto the way that goeth down from Jerusalem unto Gaza, which is desert."

Modern Corruption

Advancement is treated as the product of position, patronage, and self-promotion, so that the psalm which denies every earthly source of promotion is quietly reversed into a doctrine of ambition.

expand to see more

Psa 75:6 is a direct assault on the assumption that governs most of a man's working life: that promotion is a thing to be engineered. The psalmist canvasses the compass and finds it in no quarter, and the answer he gives is not that advancement is unimportant but that its source is a Person. God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another. The corruption is not usually a stated doctrine; it is a practical creed, visible in the energy men spend on visibility and the anxiety they carry about being overlooked. Scripture's counter-command is exact and unfashionable: humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time. The exalting is promised, and it is dated by Someone else.

There is a second and opposite error, which reads such texts as a rebuke to diligence and turns the doctrine of providence into an excuse for passivity — if God alone promotes, effort is presumption. Scripture makes no such inference. Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings. Joseph administered Egypt, Daniel served in a pagan court, and Paul laboured more abundantly than they all. The difference is not between working and not working but between working as a man who must secure his own future and working as a servant whose future is secured, who can therefore take the desert road when he is sent down it (Act 8:26) without calculating what it costs his prospects.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew negeb is the dry or parched land, and as a proper noun the Negeb south of Judah; tēmān is the right hand, hence the south; dārōm is the bright quarter. Greek notos is the south wind and the south.

expand to see more

Hebrew negeb (H5045) — parched ground, the dry country; the region south of Judah, and by extension the southern quarter.

Hebrew tēmān (H8486) — the right hand, hence the south, the observer being conceived as facing the sunrise.

Hebrew dārōm (H1864) — the south, probably the bright or sunny quarter; used chiefly in Ezekiel and Deuteronomy.

Greek notos (G3558) — the south wind, and the south quarter; the queen of the south (Mat 12:42) and they shall come from the south (Luk 13:29).

Greek mesēmbria (G3314) — midday, and hence the south; the word behind go toward the south in Act 8:26, which may also be read at noon.

Usage

"Of the dry country of the patriarchs: Abram went up out of Egypt... into the south (Gen 13:1)."

"Of the source of advancement: promotion cometh neither from the east, nor from the west, nor from the south (Psa 75:6)."

"Of the gathering to the feast: they shall come from the east, and from the west, and from the north, and from the south (Luk 13:29)."
